content_voiceover: This slide organizes hemolysis causes by where destruction happens, a great framework for boards. Intravascular hemolysis causes include mechanical fragmentation — think MAHA and prosthetic valves — hemolytic transfusion reactions, paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, infections like malaria and clostridial sepsis, chemical or toxin exposures such as arsine gas or venom, thermal injury, and G6PD deficiency, which classically causes intravascular hemolysis during oxidative stress. Extravascular hemolysis causes cluster into membrane defects like hereditary spherocytosis and elliptocytosis, metabolic defects like pyruvate kinase deficiency, environmental causes such as infection, drug-induced or immune-mediated hemolysis, and HUS, plus abnormal or unstable hemoglobins. The photos at the bottom show the classic bedside clues to intravascular hemolysis — hemoglobinuria produces dark tea colored urine, hemoglobinemia turns the plasma pink to red, and hemosiderin deposits appear as blue granules in sloughed renal tubular epithelial cells on urinalysis, a sign of chronic intravascular hemolysis like PNH.
keypoints: Intravascular: MAHA, transfusion reaction, PNH, PCH, malaria, G6PD
Extravascular: HS/HE, PK deficiency, AIHA, HUS, hemoglobinopathies
Hemosiderinuria (blue granules) = chronic intravascular hemolysis, e.g. PNH
keypoint_voiceover: Sort hemolysis causes by site. Intravascular includes mechanical fragmentation, transfusion reactions, PNH, PCH, malaria, and G6PD deficiency. Extravascular includes membrane defects like hereditary spherocytosis, metabolic defects like PK deficiency, and immune-mediated causes. Remember the bedside clues — hemoglobinuria and hemoglobinemia signal intravascular hemolysis, and hemosiderin granules in urine sediment indicate chronic intravascular hemolysis, classically seen in PNH.
